newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Grain-Prices high in eventful week.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Grain-Prices high in eventful week.

text.p: Australian grain prices continued to firm in an eventful period last week.
The Australian Wheat Board (AWB) boosted its estimate of the current Australian wheat crop to 23 million tonnes, up from the previous record of 22 million tonnes in 1983/84.
It increased its pool price by A$3 a tonne to A$188 for benchmark Australian Standard White (ASW), less than generally expected but enough to keep a floor under the market.
And it continued to perform well on the world export market, clinching a further 150,000 tonne sale to Iraq for March.
On Friday the AWB said it expected to sell up to 200,000 tonnes a month to Iraq from April onwards.
The big harvest was almost complete across Australia last week, with shipments proceeding well.

In New South Wales, Australia's biggest wheat-producing state this year with an expected harvest of eight million tonnes, shipments are well underway with slightly more than one million tonnes moved through the state's ports between November and last week.
Shipments in normal years do not begin until January. This year's performance is well ahead of schedule.

The virtual end of the harvest and the smooth operation of grain handling and shipping focused attention on prices, and by week end divergent views on the current structure of Australian wheat prices had become a main feature of the market.

While Chicago wheat futures fell throughout most of last week, Sydney wheat futures staged an almost uninterrupted rise, with the March 1977 contract gaining A$2.50 to close the week on A$169 a tonne. Other near-term contracts also rose, with May adding A$6.50 to A$170 and July A$5.50 to A$168.
By Thursday, Australian brokers were saying Sydney wheat futures were at a significant premium to Chicago. After Friday's further rise, brokers were puzzled.
Analysts agreed that the pool price, which the trade sees as sometimes used by the AWB as a tool to help keep wheat prices high, was propping futures up.
Even so, gaps still existed between high futures prices and the cash and pool prices, brokers said.
Grain trade sources saw the various prices as more in line with each other than than did brokers, but also wondered how long the AWB would be able to keep its current pool open.

Closure of the pool is widely expected to cause a significant drop in domestic prices, although a current spate of dry weather in Australia's eastern states is also helping put a floor under grains prices. This raises questions about the extent of price falls on a near-term pool closure.

Mark Martin of Agracom Risk Management said Chicago's slide would increase pressure on the AWB to close the pool. Bill Mitchell of New England Agricultural Traders said the dry weather was playing a part in Australia's rising grains market, with price rises of about A$5 a tonne over the past week occurring across the grains spectrum.
Guy Allen of GrainCorp saw the falling Australian dollar as one factor behind last week's firming domestic market in the face of sliding prices overseas.

Allen described the domestic cash market last week as firmer in light and choppy trade, with cash wheat prices up by A$6-A$8 to A$165 for ASW Newcastle. A feature of the domestic market last week was a strong rise in the Newcastle sorghum price, by about A$10 to about A$150 a tonne. The rise was attributed to lack of supply in feed wheat and to the dry weather.
